# 31 Esophageal Cancer Diagnosis and Staging

## Epidemiology & Demographics

- **Incidence & Mortality**
  - ~20,640 new US cases annually; ~16,410 deaths
  - 604,000 global new cases; 544,000 deaths (2020)
  - 7th most common cancer, 6th leading cause of cancer death worldwide
- **Histologic Trends**
  - ~90% globally: Squamous Cell Carcinoma (SCC)
  - US: Adenocarcinoma (AC) incidence surpassing SCC
  - SCC 3× more frequent in Blacks vs Caucasians
- **Risk Factors & Survival**
  - SCC: Smoking, alcohol, genetic predisposition
  - AC: GERD, Barrett’s esophagus, obesity, diabetes, Parkinson’s, eczema
  - Overall 5-year survival: ~20%

## Anatomy & Lymphatic Drainage

- **Structure & Dimensions**
  - 20–30 cm length; posterior mediastinum
  - Three natural constrictions: cricopharyngeus, broncho-aortic, GEJ
  - Layers: Mucosa (stratified squamous), submucosa, muscularis propria, adventitia
- **Anatomic Divisions** (measured from incisors)
  - Cervical: 15 to <20 cm
  - Upper thoracic: 20 to <25 cm
  - Middle thoracic: 25 to <30 cm
  - Lower thoracic: 30 to 40 cm

## Anatomy & Lymphatic Drainage

- **Lymphatics & Metastasis**
  - Rich submucosal network → longitudinal & transverse spread
  - Drains to cervical, tracheobronchial, mediastinal, gastric, celiac nodes
  - Common distant sites: liver, lungs, adrenal, retroperitoneal nodes

## Staging Nomenclature

- **Clinical Stage (cTNM)**
  - Pretreatment: physical exam, imaging, endoscopy, biopsies
- **Pathologic Stage (pTNM)**
  - Postsurgical: adds histologic exam of resected tissue
- **Post-Therapy Stage**
  - Neoadjuvant: `ycTNM` (clinical) or `ypTNM` (pathologic)
- **Residual Tumor (R Status)**
  - R0: No residual tumor
  - R1: Microscopic residual
  - R2: Macroscopic residual
  - *Note:* US (CAP) defines R1 as tumor at margin; UK defines R1 as tumor ≤1 mm from margin

## Histologic Type & Tumor Grade

- **Primary Subtypes**
  - **SCC:** Keratinocyte-like cells, intercellular bridges; often more sensitive to chemoradiation
  - **AC:** Glandular differentiation, arises from Barrett’s; better long-term prognosis post-resection
  - **ASC (Adeno-squamous):** Rare, mixed differentiation, aggressive behavior
- **Tumor Grade (G)**
  - Reflects differentiation & growth potential
  - GX: Undetermined
  - G1: Well-differentiated (low)
  - G2: Moderately differentiated (intermediate)
  - G3: Poorly differentiated/undifferentiated (high)
  - *8th Ed Update:* G4 eliminated; undifferentiated grouped into G3

## TNM Classification: T Stage

- **Depth of Invasion**
  - TX/T0: Cannot assess / No evidence
  - Tis: High-grade dysplasia
  - T1a: Lamina propria or muscularis mucosa
  - T1b: Submucosa
  - T2: Muscularis propria
  - T3: Adventitia
  - T4: Adjacent structures
    - T4a: Resectable (pleura, pericardium, diaphragm, peritoneum, azygos vein)
    - T4b: Unresectable (aorta, vertebral body, trachea)
- **Clinical Utility:** Guides resectability, multimodality planning, and prognosis

## TNM Classification: N & M Stages

- **Nodal Classification (N)**
  - N0: No positive nodes
  - N1: 1–2 involved nodes
  - N2: 3–6 involved nodes
  - N3: ≥7 involved nodes
  - *Key:* Number of nodes examined predicts survival; ≥30 nodes optimal
- **Metastasis (M)**
  - M0: No distant metastases
  - M1: Distant metastases present
- **Note:** T, N, M criteria apply uniformly to cervical, thoracic, and GEJ tumors ≤2 cm from cardia, regardless of histology

## 8th Edition AJCC/UICC Updates

- **T Category**
  - T4a expanded to include peritoneum & azygos vein
  - T1 subdivided into T1a/T1b (used for pathologic & post-neoadjuvant staging)
- **N Category**
  - N3 disease now staged as Stage IVA (any T)
  - Nodal burden classification retained
- **Other Updates**
  - G4 removed; undifferentiated → G3
  - Tumor Location (L) introduced to subcategorize pT3 SCC
  - Separate stage groups for clinical, pathologic, and post-neoadjuvant settings

## Stage Groupings & Prognostic Factors

- **Histology-Specific Groupings**
  - SCC & AC staged differently due to survival disparities
  - Early/intermediate SCC has worse survival than similarly staged AC
- **Key Modifiers**
  - Grade differentiation (G1–G3) splits Stage I into IA/IB (SCC) and IA/IB/IC (AC)
  - Location stratifies pT3 SCC and excludes T2 (previously included)
- **Post-Neoadjuvant Staging**
  - ypT0–T2 grouped together; staging depends primarily on ypN status
  - Histology has less prognostic impact after neoadjuvant therapy

## GEJ Tumors & Anatomic Location

- **Siewert Classification (Historical)**
  - Type I: Epicenter 1–5 cm above GEJ (distal esophagus)
  - Type II: Epicenter within 1 cm proximal to 2 cm distal of GEJ (cardia)
  - Type III: Epicenter 2–5 cm below GEJ, infiltrating upward
- **AJCC 8th Edition Rule**
  - Epicenters no more than 2 cm in the gastric cardia → Staged as **Esophageal Cancer**
  - \>2 cm distal to GEJ → Staged as **Gastric Cancer**

## GEJ Tumors & Anatomic Location

::: {.columns}
:::{.column width="50%"}
- Epicenter of the tumor is determined from the upper and lower borders of the
tumor length
- Its essential for the surgical resection to know the **upper border for the cervical and upper thoracic tumors** and the **lower border for cancers of the lower esophagus and GEJ**.

:::

:::{.column width="50%"}
- **Clinical Impact:** Epicenter determination critical for treatment pathway & staging algorithm

## Diagnostic Tools: Initial Evaluation

- **Upper GI Contrast Studies**
  - Historically used as "roadmap" for dysphagia
  - Identifies strictures with mucosal irregularity, polypoid tumor, apple-core constrictions
  - Double contrast barium studies: limited PPV (~42%); largely replaced by endoscopy
- **Flexible Upper Endoscopy**
  - Gold standard for visualization & tissue acquisition
  - Reports: esophageal lumen/tumor morphology, distance from incisors, length of lesion, circumferential involvement, position in relation to GEJ, skip lesions,  Barrett’s (presence/location/length)
  - **Biopsy Protocol:** ≥6 samples → ~100% diagnostic yield; avoid necrotic/fibrotic zones
  - Brush cytology useful for tight strictures; perform before biopsy
  - EUS: where standard biopsy or brushings do not yield a diagnosis in cases with high suspicion

## FDG-PET/CT Staging

- **Mechanism & Utility**
  - Detects metabolically active tissue via 18F-FDG uptake
  - Integrated PET/CT aligns functional & anatomic data
  - High accuracy for distant nodal and visceral metastases
  - SUV (standardized uptake value)
- **Performance**
  - Primary tumor sensitivity: 78–95% (false negatives in T1/T2)
  - Nodal staging: Poor sensitivity (38–82%), high specificity (76–95%)
  - Changes management in 3–20% of cases; upstages occult M1 disease
- **Limitations**
  - Not recommended for early-stage (Tis/T1) disease
  - Poor spatial resolution for juxta-tumoral nodes

## CT Scan & MRI

- **CT Scan (First-Line)**
  - Esophageal wall >5 mm = abnormal
  - Excellent for excluding T4 invasion (fat plane obliteration, >90° aortic contact)
  - Nodal criteria (pathologic nodes): Size-based (>1 cm intrathoracic/abdominal; >0.5 cm supraclavicular, >0.6cm retrocrural)
  - Limited sensitivity for distant mets (37–66%); inferior for peritoneal disease
- **MRI**
  - Multiplanar imaging; high-resolution T2 & diffusion-weighted sequences
  - T-stage accuracy: ~60% (conventional) → 81% (high-res); T3/T4 detection >95%
  - Similar nodal limitations as CT

## Endoscopic Ultrasound (EUS) & FNA

- **T Staging**
  - Visualizes 5 esophageal wall layers
  - Accuracy improves with deeper tumors (T3/T4: ~86%)
  - Struggles with T1a vs T1b differentiation; operator-dependent
  - Over-staging risk from peritumoral inflammation
- **N Staging & FNA**
  - Identifies suspicious nodes + cytologic confirmation via FNA
  - Sensitivity/Specificity/Accuracy >85% for locoregional nodes
  - FNA indicated for celiac, porta hepatis, cervical, upper thoracic adenopathy
  - Avoid FNA when primary tumor obstructs needle path

## Endoscopic Mucosal Resection (EMR)

- **Role in Staging & Therapy**
  - Resects mucosa ± submucosa down to muscularis propria
  - Provides definitive histology: depth, lymphovascular invasion, differentiation
  - Highly effective for differentiating cT1a from cT1b
- **Clinical Indications**
  - T1aN0 lesions: <2% nodal risk → EMR preferred over surgery
  - T1b or deeper: Requires esophagectomy + lymphadenectomy
- **Limitations**
  - High inter-pathologist variability in depth assessment (~48% discordance)
  - Piecemeal resection complicates margin evaluation

## Bronchoscopy & EBUS

- **Flexible Bronchoscopy**
  - Evaluates mid/upper esophageal tumors for airway invasion
  - Signs of invasion: widened carina, external compression, fistula
  - Biopsy/cytology required; visual bulging often benign
- **Endobronchial Ultrasound (EBUS)**
  - Assesses tracheobronchial wall integrity (adventitia disruption)
  - Superior to CT/MRI/bronchoscopy alone (Sensitivity 92%, Specificity 83%)
  - Combined EBUS + EUS reduces false-positive nodal FNA results
  - Upstages ~12% of patients; valuable for peri-tracheal/subcarinal nodes

## Laparoscopy & Thoracoscopy

- **Diagnostic Role**
  - Detects occult intraperitoneal/intrathoracic metastases missed by CT/PET
  - Samples regional nodes; assesses liver surface & peritoneal cavity
  - Particularly valuable for distal esophageal/GEJ adenocarcinomas
- **Impact & Limitations**
  - Changes staging in ~32% of AC cases
  - Upstages nodal status in 0–21%, downstages in 4–19%
  - Requires general anesthesia, longer OR time; role diminishing with improved PET/CT
  - Reserved for highly selected cases with suspicious imaging

## Therapy Monitoring & Restaging

- **Post-Neoadjuvant Assessment**
  - NCCN recommends FDG-PET/CT, contrast CT, endoscopy ± biopsy
- **Modality Limitations**
  - **CT:** Morphologic only; 35% sensitivity for pathologic response
  - **EUS:** Poor reproducibility; invasive; limited by post-radiation changes
  - **Endoscopic Biopsy:** ~50% accuracy; bite-on-bite technique improves sensitivity to 74%
- **FDG-PET/CT Utility**
  - Moderate accuracy (Sens 62%, Spec 73%)
  - Detects interval metastases in ~10%
  - Cannot reliably distinguish residual tumor from inflammation

## Surveillance Strategy Post-Therapy

- **Clinical Reality**
  - Salvage rate after recurrence is low (~2%)
  - Differentiating fibrosis vs residual disease remains challenging
  - Active surveillance considered for complete responders unfit/unwilling for surgery
- **NCCN Consensus Guidelines**
  1. H&P every 3–6 months (years 1–3), then every 6 months (years 4–5), then annually
  2. CBC & chemistry as clinically indicated
  3. Imaging & endoscopy as clinically indicated
  4. Dilation for anastomotic stenosis
  5. Nutritional counseling
- *Future:* Liquid biopsy & molecular tools may improve preclinical recurrence detection

## Future Directions & Standardization

- **9th Edition Expectations**
  - Precision surgical treatment & individualized staging
  - Enhanced post-neoadjuvant prognostic modeling
- **Pathology & Reporting Standardization**
  - Adopt modified Ryan Tumor Regression Grading (TRG) system
  - Uniform circumferential resection margin criteria (CAP vs UK)
  - Report distance to margin (mm) & separate nodal yield by region
- **Emerging Technologies**
  - Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) for minimal residual disease monitoring
  - Advanced functional imaging & AI-assisted staging
  - Integration into national registries (e.g., ESODATA) for quality improvement

## Summary & Key Takeaways

- Accurate staging dictates multimodality vs endoscopic vs surgical pathways
- 8th Edition TNM integrates histology, grade, location, and nodal burden
- Diagnostic algorithm: Endoscopy/Biopsy → CT/PET → EUS/FNA → EMR (if early) → Laparoscopy/EBUS (selected)
- Post-neoadjuvant restaging remains imperfect; PET/CT & bite-on-bite biopsy show promise
- Multidisciplinary tumor board review is essential for optimal management
- Ongoing standardization in TRG, margins, and liquid biopsy will refine precision care
